name: PHP
year_note: Rasmus Lerdorf wrote the Personal Home Page Tools in 1994 and released their source on 8 June 1995; the 'Forms Interpreter' followed that September and the combined name PHP/FI dates from 1996. PHP 3 (1998), a rewrite by Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski, is the direct ancestor of today's language.
tagline: The server-side language that grew out of HTML templates to run much of the Web, from PHP/FI to typed, JIT-compiled PHP 8.
summary: PHP is a dynamically typed scripting language designed for generating web pages on the server: code is embedded between `<?php ?>` tags in HTML and each request runs in a fresh, shared-nothing environment. Starting as a set of personal CGI tools, it became the easiest way to put a database-backed site online and still powers platforms such as WordPress and MediaWiki. Modern PHP (7 and 8) adds optional runtime-checked type declarations, a Java-like class model with traits, enums, `match` expressions, readonly properties and a JIT compiler.
history:
Rasmus Lerdorf wrote a set of CGI binaries in C in 1994 to track visits to his online résumé and released them as the 'Personal Home Page Tools' in June 1995; that September he added a Forms Interpreter, and the combined PHP/FI (version 2.0 final in November 1997) let users embed simple scripts in HTML. In 1997 Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski of Tel Aviv began rewriting the parser, and PHP 3 (June 1998) — with the recursive name 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor' and an extension API — became the version that took off. Their Zend Engine powered PHP 4 (2000), and PHP 5 (2004) introduced a new object model with visibility, interfaces and exceptions.

An ambitious Unicode-based PHP 6 was abandoned, and PHP 7 (2015) instead delivered the 'phpng' engine rewrite, which roughly doubled throughput on WordPress-based benchmarks, along with scalar and return type declarations. PHP 8.0 (2020) added a JIT compiler, union types, named arguments, attributes and the `match` expression; 8.1 (2021) brought enums, readonly properties and fibers; later releases added readonly classes (8.2), property hooks (8.4) and the pipe operator `|>` (8.5, 2025). The PHP Foundation, founded in 2021, funds core development.
innovations: Code embedded directly in HTML pages and processed per request on the server, making dynamic web pages accessible to non-specialists
A shared-nothing execution model: every HTTP request starts from a clean state, which made cheap shared hosting and horizontal scaling simple
One ordered hash map ('array') serving as list, dictionary, set and record
Optional type declarations enforced at run time in a dynamic language (PHP 7), with a per-file strict_types switch between coercion and strict checking
A comprehensive built-in web toolkit — request superglobals, sessions, database drivers — in the standard distribution

typing.notes: Parameter, return and property types (7.0+) are checked at run time, coercing scalars unless `declare(strict_types=1)`; class types are nominal, untyped code is duck-typed. Static analysers (PHPStan, Psalm) add ahead-of-time checking and docblock generics.

influenced_by.note: $-prefixed variables, associative arrays, string interpolation and Perl-compatible regular expressions (preg_*); PHP took over Perl's CGI niche.
Brace syntax, operators, and many function names and signatures taken from the C library (printf, strlen, strcmp...); the engine is written in C.
The PHP 5 object model: interfaces, abstract and final classes, visibility modifiers and exceptions.

structured-control.note: Also alternative colon syntax (`foreach (...): ... endforeach;`) for templates.

exceptions.note: try/catch/finally (finally since 5.5); errors are also exceptions (Error/Throwable) since 7.0.

coroutines.note: Fibers are full stackful coroutines, used by async libraries such as Amp and ReactPHP; generators can also receive values via send() (5.5).

gradual-typing.note: Class type hints since 5.0; scalar and return types in 7.0, typed properties in 7.4, union types in 8.0. Checked at run time rather than compile time.

classes.note: Basic classes since PHP 3; the PHP 5 object model (2004) added visibility, abstract/final classes and objects passed by handle. Enums (8.1) and readonly classes (8.2) extend it.

inheritance.note: Single inheritance plus interfaces and traits.

traits-mixins.note: `trait` with `use`, including conflict resolution via insteadof/as.

abstract-data-types.note: private/protected members; readonly properties (8.1) and asymmetric visibility (8.4).

modules.note: Namespaces plus include/require; in practice Composer's PSR-4 autoloading acts as the module system.

first-class-functions.note: Anonymous functions (5.3), arrow functions `fn` (7.4) and first-class callable syntax `strlen(...)` (8.1); earlier code passed function names as strings.

closures.note: Captured variables are listed explicitly with `use (...)`; `fn` arrow functions capture by value automatically.

garbage-collection.note: A cycle collector supplements reference counting.

reference-counting.note: Values are reference counted, with copy-on-write for arrays and strings.

reflection.note: The Reflection API, plus attributes (8.0) readable through it.

regex-builtin.note: Bundled PCRE functions (preg_match, preg_replace); patterns are ordinary strings with delimiters.

milestones.event: Rasmus Lerdorf releases the Personal Home Page Tools (8 June)
PHP/FI 2.0 released; Gutmans and Suraski begin rewriting the parser
PHP 3.0: 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor' and an extensible core
PHP 5.0: new object model with interfaces, visibility and exceptions
PHP 7.0: phpng engine, scalar and return type declarations
PHP 8.0: JIT, union types, named arguments, attributes, match
PHP 8.1: enums, readonly properties, fibers; PHP Foundation founded
PHP 8.4: property hooks and asymmetric visibility

trivia: 'PHP' originally stood for 'Personal Home Page'; since PHP 3 it officially means the recursive acronym 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf's first tools were CGI binaries written in C to log visits to his online résumé.

hello.notes: Text outside `<?php` tags is copied to the output verbatim, so a file containing only `Hello, World!` would also work. The closing `?>` is conventionally omitted in pure-PHP files.

factorial.code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function factorial(int $n): int
{
    return $n <= 1 ? 1 : $n * factorial($n - 1);
}

echo factorial(10), "\n";
factorial.notes: With `strict_types=1`, calling factorial("10") throws a TypeError instead of coercing the string. Integers overflow to float beyond PHP_INT_MAX.

fizzbuzz.notes: `match (true)` returns the first arm whose condition is identical (===) to true. Unlike switch, match is an expression, compares strictly, never falls through and throws if no arm matches.

higher-order.notes: Note the historical argument-order mismatch: array_filter(array, callback) but array_map(callback, array). array_filter keeps the original keys (1, 3, 5...), which implode ignores.

shapes.code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

interface Shape
{
    public function area(): int;
}

final readonly class Rectangle implements Shape
{
    public function __construct(public int $width, public int $height) {}

    public function area(): int { return $this->width * $this->height; }
}

final readonly class Triangle implements Shape
{
    public function __construct(public int $base, public int $height) {}

    public function area(): int { return intdiv($this->base * $this->height, 2); }
}

foreach ([new Rectangle(3, 4), new Triangle(10, 3)] as $shape) {
    printf("%s: %d\n", $shape::class, $shape->area());
}
shapes.notes: Constructor property promotion (8.0) declares and assigns the properties in the constructor signature, and a readonly class (8.2) makes every property write-once. `$shape::class` yields the object's class name.

signature.notes: Everything outside `<?php ?>` is emitted as-is and `<?= $x ?>` echoes a value — PHP's original job as a hypertext preprocessor. A newline directly after `?>` is swallowed, so the loop tags leave no blank lines. The backed enum and exhaustive `match` are PHP 8.1/8.0 features; htmlspecialchars escapes user data.
